/-!
# Erdős Problem 695
*Reference:* [erdosproblems.com/695](https://www.erdosproblems.com/695)
-/

@[expose] public section

open Filter Finset Real

namespace Erdos695

/--
Let $q_1 < q_2 < \cdots$ be a sequence of primes such that $q_{i + 1} \equiv 1 \pmod{q_i}$. Is it
true that
$$
\lim_{k \to \infty} q_k^{1/k} = \infty?
$$
-/
@[category research open, AMS 11]
theorem erdos_695 : answer(sorry) ↔
    ∀ {q : ℕ → ℕ},
      StrictMono q →
      (∀ i, (q i).Prime) →
      (∀ i, q (i + 1) % q i = 1) →
      Tendsto (fun k => (q k : ℝ) ^ (1 / k : ℝ)) atTop atTop := by
  sorry

/--
Is there a sequence of primes $q_1 < q_2 < \cdots$ such that $q_{i + 1} \equiv 1 \pmod{q_i}$ and
$$
q(k) \leq \exp(k (\log k)^{1 + o(1)})?
$$
-/
@[category research open, AMS 11]
theorem erdos_695.variants.upperBound : answer(sorry) ↔
    ∃ q : ℕ → ℕ,
      StrictMono q ∧
      (∀ i, (q i).Prime) ∧
      (∀ i, q (i + 1) % q i = 1) ∧
      ∃ o : ℕ → ℝ,
        (o =o[atTop] (1 : ℕ → ℝ)) ∧
        -- We use `(k + 1)` here as the informal statement is 1-indexed.
        ∀ k, q k ≤ exp ((k + 1) * log (k + 1) ^ (1 + o k)) := by
  sorry

end Erdos695

reformulations.difference: Relative to the one-indexed formulation in the docstring, the zero-indexed Lean sequence uses exponent 1/k rather than 1/(k+1).
reformulations.equivalence_argument: For k ≥ 1 and a = q k ≥ 2, (a^(1/k))^(1/2) ≤ a^(1/(k+1)) ≤ a^(1/k). Consequently either root sequence tends to +∞ exactly when the other does. At k = 0, Lean evaluates the root expression to 1, which cannot affect the limit. This equivalence was proved as root_index_shift_iff; exact source-formula verification remains subject to the limitation below.

reformulations.difference: Lean requires the bound at every index, rather than eventually as an asymptotic bound is ordinarily understood. The initial bound forces q 0 = 2 and o 0 = -1.
reformulations.equivalence_argument: This does not change the existence question described in the docstring. Given an eventually bounded prime chain, replace only its first prime by 2. The next prime is odd and greater than 2, so all chain conditions survive. Set the error at index 0 to -1, giving the valid bound 2 ≤ exp 1. For each other exceptional index k ≥ 1, log(k+1) is positive and unequal to 1, so a suitable real exponent makes the bound hold. Changing finitely many error values preserves o → 0, equivalently o =o[atTop] 1. The converse is immediate. The full existential equivalence was proved as upperBound_equivalence; exact source-formula verification remains subject to the limitation below.
